analysis.one_liner: Makes breast implant manufacturers pay to surgically remove implants and funds safety research on silicone.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced with 24 bipartisan sponsors in December 1995, it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every breast implant maker to notify women who received silicone gel or saline implants before 1994 and pay the full cost of surgical removal, including follow-up care, scar tissue removal, and mammograms, with the patient choosing the doctor and hospital. It also directed federal research on the health effects of silicone and other chemicals in implants, required a standardized informed-consent form before any silicone implant, and barred doctors from refusing care to implant recipients. It never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly hundreds of thousands of women who received silicone implants before 1994 and wanted them removed would have had the surgery, including pre- and post-operative care and related treatment, paid by the manufacturer rather than out of pocket, with freedom to pick their own physician and facility. Future patients would get a standardized warning form, and implant recipients would gain legal protection against doctors refusing them treatment.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must notify every woman with a pre-1994 silicone or saline implant and pay all medical, surgical, and hospital costs of removal at her request, including follow-up surgery for residual silicone, scar capsules, and granulomas, plus mammograms and medication [S3].
Patients choose their own physician and hospital or surgery center for the removal, and the removed implant becomes the patient's property [S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services must conduct or commission research on the physiological, neurological, and immunological effects of silicone toxicity and other chemicals used in implant manufacturing [S2].

No physician may perform a silicone implant without the patient signing a federally prescribed consent form disclosing all health risks, and no physician may refuse to treat a patient because she has an implant [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Breast implant manufacturers would bear the full cost of removal surgeries, follow-up care, and mammograms for anyone with a pre-1994 implant who requests removal, plus the cost of publishing nationwide notices. Organ procurement organizations and blood collectors would face losing federal grants or licenses if they accept donations from implant recipients.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars federal grants to organ procurement organizations and licenses to blood collectors if they accept donations from anyone with a breast implant, which would deny implant recipients the ability to donate organs or blood and could shrink the donation supply [S3].

Requiring manufacturers to fund removal for every pre-1994 implant, on request and with no medical screening, could push some women into surgery they may not need, since by the mid-1990s large studies were beginning to question how strong the link between implants and systemic disease actually was (general medical context).

Open-ended manufacturer-funded removal would carry a large, hard-to-estimate cost for implant makers, an industry already facing heavy implant litigation in the mid-1990s, raising the chance of firms exiting the market (general context).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women who wanted their implants out, this was a strong deal: the manufacturer, not the patient, pays, and the patient picks the surgeon. The design flaws are real, though. The organ and blood donation bans in Section 6 punish implant recipients themselves and could reduce donation supply, and a blanket right to manufacturer-funded removal, with no medical criteria, invites unnecessary surgeries and open-ended costs. A better bill would have dropped the donation bans and tied removal funding to medical need.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. James Traficant introduced the Breast Implant Accountability Act on December 15, 1995, joined by nine original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced, and three days later, on December 18, 1995, to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment [S5].
It gathered 23 cosponsors, 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans [S4].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in the subcommittee when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Breast implant manufacturers are better off: the bill died, so they never had to pay for removal surgeries, follow-up care, or nationwide notices for women with pre-1994 implants. Women who wanted manufacturer-funded removal got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided: 20 Democrats and 3 Republicans backed the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the merits is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have made them pay full removal costs, follow-up care, and mammograms for every pre-1994 implant recipient who requested it. The bill's death left them bearing no such costs at a time when the industry faced extensive implant litigation.

Manufacturer-funded removals would have generated a stream of paid surgeries, but the standardized informed-consent requirement and the removal mandate would have curtailed and complicated new silicone implant procedures.

industries.industry: Blood collection and organ procurement organizations
industries.note: They would have lost federal grants or licenses for accepting donations from implant recipients, forcing them to turn such donors away. The rule protects against perceived contamination risk but penalizes both the organizations and the recipients.
